historical_commentary.text: This note is the second in a series building an end-user-customizable output form, extending an earlier note by persisting the user's chosen columns and other preference variables into a database table rather than only holding them in memory for the session. The specific technique — storing UI preferences as discrete fields in a classic-language preferences table — is a pattern that still works today but has since been largely superseded by storing preferences as a single JSON object/BLOB, which is far more flexible for arbitrary, evolving preference sets.
related_updates: Modern 4D applications typically persist user preferences as JSON objects (via JSON Stringify/Parse or 4D's object storage) rather than as individual table fields
ORDA and the object/collection data types introduced in later 4D versions make storing flexible, schema-less preference structures far simpler than the classic per-column table approach shown here
